ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute bronchitis is a self‑limited inflammation of the bronchi, usually viral, presenting with cough and sputum. It is diagnosed clinically, managed supportively, and complications are rare.

sections.p: Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchi lasting less than 3 weeks, usually viral. Diagnosis is clinical: cough >3 days, sputum, no evidence of pneumonia.
Severity is gauged by symptom burden and impact on daily life. Mild: cough only; moderate: cough + fatigue; severe: cough + dyspnea or hypoxia.
The majority are viral infections. Bacterial causes are uncommon and usually secondary.
b: Viruses: RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus

sections.p: Patients have a dry or productive cough, often worse in the morning. Sputum may be clear or yellow. Fever is usually low grade or absent.
Investigations are reserved for atypical or severe cases.

t.b: Normal or mild infiltrate; abnormal suggests alternative diagnosis

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be serious.
Treat the underlying cause and provide supportive care. Antibiotics are reserved for bacterial infection.
b: Cough suppressants: dextromethorphan for dry cough

sections.p: Most recover in 2–3 weeks. Prevention focuses on hand hygiene and avoiding smoking.
Conditions that mimic acute bronchitis include pneumonia, asthma exacerbation, COPD flare, and pertussis.
Normal chest X‑ray can miss early pneumonia; low‑grade fever may be present in viral infections.
b: Chest X‑ray may be normal in early pneumonia
Low‑grade fever common in viral bronchitis

faq.q: Is antibiotics always needed for acute bronchitis?
faq.a: No, antibiotics are reserved for suspected bacterial infection.

faq.q: Can I use cough syrup for a dry cough?
faq.a: Yes, a dextromethorphan‑based syrup can help, but avoid if the cough is productive.

faq.q: When should I get a chest X‑ray?
faq.a: When there is fever >38°C, chest pain, or worsening dyspnea.

exam: Explain why antibiotics are not routinely prescribed for acute bronchitis.
Describe the clinical features that would prompt you to order a chest X‑ray.
